newsitem.title: FRANCE: More payments found in Elf deal - report.
newsitem.headline: More payments found in Elf deal - report.

text.p: Over $50 million in secret commissions allegedly were paid by French oil giant Elf Aquitaine in connection with its purchase of a former East German refinery, two French newspapers said on Tuesday.

However, Swiss and French investigators looking into Elf's 1992 purchase of the Leuna refinery have so far been unable to trace the payments to their ultimate recipients, according to reports in the Liberation and Le Monde dailies.
In particular, the probes have turned up no proof that any of the payments found their way into the coffers of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union, according to the reports.
"The sums are exhorbitant, the paths they follow are opaque," Genevieve Gomez, a former aide to Elf chairman Philippe Jaffre, was quoted as saying by Liberation.
Previous reports have spoken of alleged secret payments totalling just 13.5 million marks ($7.9 million).
The CDU has flatly denied media reports that it took bribes in connection with the deal, and the Paris public prosecutor's office said last month that it had no evidence of covert payments.

Le Monde said probes in France and Switzerland had so far been unable to track the secret payments because they had been paid via Swiss bank accounts to shell corporations, which then passed them on to unknown recipients.
A spokesman for Elf declined to comment on the latest reports.
The Leuna plant was acquired from the Treuhandanstalt, an agency of the German government in charge of privatising the former communist state's industries.
The Elf case began as a French investigation of alleged financial irregularities when Loik Le Floch-Prigent was chairman of the state-owned oil firm in 1988-93.
It has since widened to cover Elf's operations and commission payments abroad including in Gabon and Venezuela. The probe was again widened in late April to cover suspect payments involving Germany.

Le Monde said Le Floch-Prigent pushed the deal because it was strongly supported by Kohl and France's then president Francois Mitterrand as a symbolic embrace of German reunification and Franco-German friendship.
French police are investigating the mysterious disappearance of documents relating to the case from the Paris office of investigating magistrate Eva Joly.
